title: Nurses Aid: The Effects of Arugula Extract On Cardiovascular and Endothelial Function In Overnight Healthcare Workers: A Pilot Study
official: Nurses Aid: The Effects of Arugula Extract On Cardiovascular and Endothelial Function In Overnight Healthcare Workers: A Pilot Study
summary: Overnight healthcare workers are routinely exposed to physiological and occupational stressors that may negatively affect cardiovascular and endothelial function. Chronic overnight work is associated with circadian disruption, sleep restriction, autonomic dysregulation, oxidative stress, and increased cardiovascular disease risk. Endothelial dysfunction may occur before clinically apparent cardiovascular disease and is characterized in part by impaired nitric oxide (NO) mediated vasodilation. Acute overnight work may also affect vascular function. Previous investigations in medical personnel have reported reductions in brachial artery flow-mediated dilation (FMD) following a single overnight shift, suggesting that measurable endothelial impairment may occur during the immediate post-shift period. NO is an important signaling molecule involved in the regulation of vascular tone, blood flow, and blood pressure. Under normal conditions, endothelial NO synthase produces NO from L-arginine. However, oxidative stress and impaired endothelial function can reduce NO production and bioavailability. Dietary nitrate provides an alternative pathway for NO production through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway. Following ingestion, nitrate is absorbed into the circulation and a portion is concentrated in saliva, where oral nitrate-reducing bacteria convert nitrate to nitrite. Nitrite can then be further reduced to biologically active NO. This pathway may remain functional under conditions in which endogenous endothelial NO production is impaired. Dietary nitrate supplementation has been investigated as a nutritional strategy for supporting cardiovascular and vascular function. Previous studies using nitrate-rich vegetables have demonstrated increases in circulating nitrate and nitrite, reductions in blood pressure, and improvements in endothelial function. Arugula is a nitrate-rich leafy green vegetable and contains one of the highest reported nitrate concentrations among commonly consumed leafy green and cruciferous vegetables. However, most dietary nitrate research has focused on beetroot-derived supplementation, and arugula remains underrepresented. Acute arugula extract supplementation may therefore provide a practical source of exogenous nitrate for examining vascular responses during the post-shift period. The purpose of this study is to determine the acute effects of arugula extract (AE) supplementation on cardiovascular and endothelial function following an overnight shift in healthcare workers. Specifically, the study will determine whether acute AE supplementation: 1) improves FMD, 2) increases circulating nitrate, nitrite, and total NO metabolites, and 3) reduces blood pressure compared with a post-shift control condition. Heart rate will also be assessed throughout each condition. We hypothesize that AE supplementation will increase circulating NO metabolites, improve FMD, and reduce blood pressure following an overnight healthcare shift.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Males and females between the ages of 18 and 35
* Currently Employed in a healthcare position involving direct patient care
* Regularly complete at least two 12-hour shifts per week
* Worked an overnight schedule for a minimum of six months
* Able and willing to complete two post shift experiential visits

Exclusion Criteria:

* Current use of tobacco products
* Previously diagnosed stage II hypertension, metabolic disease, or renal disease
* Current use of nitrate supplements including beetroot products or nitrate rich pre-workout supplements
* Currently taking any prescription that may affect blood pressure or heart rate
* Pregnant or planning to become pregnant
